title: The Fool Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: The Fool upright: beginnings, trust; reversed: holding back or rushing. Love, work, advice, Waite's 1911 text and the 1909 card. Draw it for your question.
image_alt: The Fool, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a young man with a white rose and a bag on a staff steps toward a cliff edge, a small white dog at his heels and a white sun above.
capsule: The Fool is card 0 of the Major Arcana: new beginnings, innocence and trust in a step not yet taken. Reversed, that step is held back by doubt or turns reckless. A hopeful card, it still asks you to watch the ground. As a yes or no question, upright leans yes: he steps forward, ready for what is new.

blocks.heading: What is on The Fool card?
paragraphs: A young man in rich, patterned clothes pauses at the edge of a cliff high in the mountains, a small white dog leaping at his heels. Waite describes him moving "with light step, as if earth and its trammels had little power to restrain him", his eyes on the open sky rather than on the drop below, and adds: "His countenance is full of intelligence and expectant dream" (p. 152).
A white sun fills the top corner behind him. Waite writes that it "knows whence he came, whither he is going" (pp. 152–155). On the 1909 card the sky is yellow and 0 is printed at the top.

He holds a rose in one hand, white on the 1909 card, and in the other a costly wand with an embroidered wallet hanging from it over his right shoulder. For Waite the edge "has no terror" for him (p. 152), and the dim signs on the wallet show "that many sub-conscious memories are stored up in the soul" (p. 161).

Older decks told a darker story. Waite recalls a Fool who "does not know that he is on the brink of a precipice", while a dog or some other animal is "attacking him from behind" (pp. 29–30). On the 1909 card nothing chases him: "his dog is still bounding" (p. 152).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about The Fool?
paragraphs: The upright words in Waite's list all name a loss of measure, from plain foolishness onward; "bewrayment" is an old word for giving yourself away. The reversed words describe the opposite trouble: not caring enough, letting things drift.

Waite himself found the fortune-telling meanings of the Major Arcana "artificial and arbitrary" (p. 287), and he saw far more in this card. He wrote that the Fool "signifies the journey outward" (p. 161) and called the young man "the spirit in search of experience" (p. 155). He also said that the right shade of the card in any reading has to be judged from the cards around it (pp. 309–310).

blocks.heading: What does The Fool mean upright?
paragraphs: New beginnings are the heart of The Fool upright: a new path, an idea you want to try, a change you feel curious about. The card also carries innocence and spontaneity, the free spirit who says yes before every answer is in. It tends to turn up when you feel excitement and uncertainty at the same time.

The card does not ask you to know where the road ends. It asks for openness: say yes to the first small step and travel light, leaving behind old plans, other people's expectations and the need to control every detail. Sometimes that step is a leap, and the card allows for it.

The cliff is the other half of the meaning. Waite's list warns of folly, and the picture places the step at the very edge, so trust works best with one eye on the ground. If this fits your situation, the card's question is simple: what first step are you ready to take?

blocks.heading: What does The Fool mean reversed?
paragraphs: A beginning stuck in one of two ways is the reversed meaning. Either you want to move and keep holding back, often out of fear of the new, or you are rushing ahead without looking. That second case is plain recklessness: risks taken without thought, a naive trust that the road will hold. The fresh start is still possible, only tangled with doubt or haste.

Waite's reversed list, with negligence, carelessness and apathy, matches the second case: a start not taken seriously, energy that drifts away. Holding back out of doubt is a modern reading, not Waite's.

Neither reading is a bad sign. If you are holding back, ask what would make the first step feel safe enough and take a smaller version of it; if you notice haste, slow down enough to see where you are going.

blocks.heading: What does The Fool mean in love?
paragraphs: Curiosity rather than a plan is how The Fool meets love: a new romance, flirting for the fun of it, feelings that are light and spontaneous. Without a partner, that can mean openness to someone new, or to a new way of meeting people, without deciding right away where it has to lead.

For a couple, the card invites freshness: something new together, new eyes for each other, fewer old expectations. It is a card of discovery more than of settling down, so commitment is not its strong side.
Reversed, the meaning turns to fear of commitment, to holding back from something you want, or to jumping in so fast that you skip over what matters to you. Which of these sounds more like you?

blocks.heading: What does The Fool mean for work and money?
paragraphs: A new start is The Fool's working meaning: a new role, a project, learning something from scratch, a wish to try a different direction. It backs curiosity and the courage to be a beginner, and the cliff adds a practical note: check the details before you commit.

For money, the card stands for a fresh start and a carefree attitude: a new source of income or a first budget of your own, and spending on impulse because something feels exciting. Waite's list has a word for that last case: "extravagance".
Reversed, the money meaning is recklessness, risky moves made without looking, or the opposite: a plan you keep postponing out of doubt.

blocks.heading: What is The Fool's advice?
paragraphs: Take one small, new step and let it be imperfect. The Fool's advice is to move before you have every answer, while still looking where you put your foot. A simple way to practice it: take a different route on a walk or commute and notice what the change shows you.

blocks.heading: Is The Fool a yes or no card?
The Fool as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: The young man at the cliff edge is the free spirit: someone who says yes to something new, travels light, trusts the road and can be a little naive about the drop. He may also be the part of you that is ready to start. As feelings, The Fool stands for new, light and playful attraction: excitement, curiosity, a crush that feels like an adventure, with no plan yet for where it goes. It is fresh interest rather than settled commitment. Reversed, the feelings turn hesitant or careless: fear of being tied down, mixed signals, an interest that runs hot and then drifts.

pairs.text: A beginning meets focus and tools. Choose one goal and put your skills to work on it.
A spark for something new. Give the idea a first small form while it is still warm.
A wish to leap beside a choice held at arm's length. Notice what you avoid looking at.
One cycle comes together as another begins. Tie off the loose end, then step forward lighter.

blocks.heading: The Fool or the Ace of Wands?
paragraphs: Both cards speak of beginnings. The Ace of Wands shows a hand from a cloud that "grasps a stout wand", and Waite gives it "principle, beginning, source" (p. 196). It is the spark itself, an idea or a burst of energy. The Fool is the person stepping onto the road, with the trust of the start and the risk of the edge. Is there energy for this? Look to the Ace. Am I ready to step into the unknown? That is The Fool's question.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about The Fool
paragraphs: What new step have I been circling, and what is the smallest version of it I could take?
What am I carrying that I could leave behind before I start?
Where do I need more trust, and where do I need to look at the ground?

faq.q: Is The Fool a good or bad card?
faq.a: Mostly good. It backs curiosity, fresh starts and the nerve to begin without a full plan. What it warns about is recklessness and naivety: enthusiasm alone never checked anyone's footing, so look before the leap.

faq.q: Does The Fool mean I am being foolish?
faq.a: Not as a judgment of you. The name is old: Waite lists the card as "The Fool, Mate, or Unwise Man" (p. 29), and his divinatory list does open with folly. Read today, the card is about starting before you are sure, which can look unwise from the outside and still be the right first move for you.

faq.q: Why is The Fool called the strongest tarot card?
faq.a: No card is officially the strongest. The reputation comes from its place outside the numbered sequence and from how much Waite saw in it: he called it "the most speaking of all the symbols" (p. 161). In an actual reading it carries the same weight as any other card.

On the 1909 card it is 0, but Waite's own book wavers. In Part I he lists the Fool as number 21 and notes that in most arrangements it is "the cipher card, number nothing" (p. 29). In Part II he places it after card 20 and adds: "Wherever it ought to be put, the Zero is an unnumbered card" (p. 161). On Arcana Diary it opens the Major Arcana, before The Magician.

waite.quote: Folly, mania, extravagance, intoxication, delirium, frenzy, bewrayment. Reversed: Negligence, absence, distribution, carelessness, apathy, nullity, vanity.
